title: Students Out of Height Order
statement:
Students stand in a line for a photo, and heights[i] is the height of the student at position i. The photographer wants them sorted from shortest to tallest (ties in any order).

Return how many positions hold a different height from the one that position would hold in the sorted line.

examples.why: Sorted is [1, 2, 2, 3, 5]. Positions 0, 1 and 3 differ; positions 2 and 4 already match.
Only one student is misplaced in spirit, but every position changes in the sorted line, and positions are what count.
Equal heights are already in order.

hints: You need the sorted line to compare against. Do you have to modify the original?
Copy, sort, and compare position by position.
Heights are at most 100. A counting sort over 100 buckets builds the sorted line in O(n) without comparisons.

explain.intuition:
The question is not "how many moves" but "how many positions differ from the sorted line", so build the sorted line and compare. A copy plus a regular sort already works.

The small range of heights invites a counting sort: count how many students have each height, then walk heights from 1 to 100, and emitting that many copies of each gives the expected line. You can compare while you emit, without storing the sorted array.
steps: Count the students of each height in an array of size 101.
Walk the line with index i and a pointer h to the smallest height whose count is still positive.
If heights[i] != h, add one to the answer. Then decrement count[h].
pitfalls: Sorting the original array in place and then comparing it with itself.
Counting students that need to move, or the number of swaps, instead of mismatched positions.
Using the default JavaScript sort() without a comparator, which sorts numbers as strings: [100, 2] stays put.

solutions.title: Sort a copy
solutions.idea: Sort a copy of the heights and count positions that differ.

solutions.title: Counting sort
solutions.idea: Count each height, then walk the counts in order to produce the expected height at each position.

followups: What is the fewest number of swaps that sorts the line? How is that a different question?
Heights are arbitrary 32-bit integers. Is counting sort still a good choice?
